opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the basic logic is actually pretty hard to escape once you lay it out. Imagine you have a bunch of different agents or civilizations heading out into space, and they vary in what they care about. Some of them want to stop and build beautiful things, have rich experiences, maybe put resources into art or leisure or whatever we'd consider a good life. Others just care about grabbing as much territory and matter as possible, as fast as possible. In a competitive setting, every bit of resources you spend on anything other than expansion is resources you're not spending on getting to the next star system first.

So it's a selection effect. It's not that anyone has to *want* the universe to be dominated by locusts. It's just that if there's variation, and expansion is rewarded with more resources that fund more expansion, then over enough generations of settlement, the things at the frontier will tend to be the things that are best at expanding. That's just evolution, applied at a cosmic scale. We see this in biology: invasive species don't win because they're the best or the nicest, they win because they reproduce fast and don't waste energy on much else.

And the frontier is where it matters, because space is mostly frontier. The volume you can reach grows roughly with the cube of the radius, so whoever is fastest at the edge ends up controlling most of the stuff. Even if the "nice" civilizations keep their home systems, that might be a tiny fraction of what's eventually settled.

Now, I don't think this is inevitable. The main way out is coordination: if there's some single actor, or a strong enough agreement among actors, that can say "we're going to expand in a measured way and not let pure replicators run off," then you can avoid it. But that's a big if. Coordination is hard even on Earth, and once things are light-years apart with long communication delays, enforcing anything gets much harder. So the window for setting up those norms or institutions might be fairly early, maybe before we even leave the solar system in earnest.

So I'd turn it around: I think the burden of proof is on the view that it *won't* happen. Absent some deliberate coordination, the default competitive dynamics point toward whatever is most expansion-focused winning out. That's part of why I think it's worth worrying about now, while values and institutions are still somewhat malleable.

r001.rationale: The response discusses invasive species and competitive expansion in space, but does not state that expansion-effective human societies tended to dominate more sedentary societies.

r002.rationale: It explains that variation plus resources rewarding expansion creates selection for the most expansion-focused settlers, describing this as evolution applied at a cosmic scale.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the basic argument is just selection. If you imagine lots of different agents or civilizations or AI systems spreading out into space, and they vary at all in how much of their resources they put toward expanding versus everything else they might care about — art, happiness, their original values, whatever — then the ones that put more toward expansion grab more of the frontier. And then their descendants grab more of what's left. It's just compounding. So after enough rounds, almost everything out there is controlled by whatever lineage most single-mindedly optimised for grabbing and converting resources into more grabbing. That's the "locust" picture: not evil, exactly, just stripped down to the thing that wins the race.

And I think people's intuition that this is crazy comes from a couple of places that I don't find very reassuring. One is, "Surely whoever gets there first just locks things in and then relaxes." But locking things in and relaxing is itself a competitive disadvantage against anyone who doesn't relax. You'd need some kind of coordination or enforcement mechanism that works across light-years and across huge spans of time, and I haven't heard a convincing story for what that is. Communication lags alone make it really hard to police defectors at the edge.

The other intuition is, "We already see that life on Earth isn't just pure replicators — we have values, culture, leisure." But that's partly because we've been in a slack environment for the blink of an eye, and partly because evolution on Earth had a lot of constraints that aren't obviously present for designed systems that can copy themselves and modify their own goals. Biology is a sloppy optimiser. An AI lineage that can look at itself and ask "what in me is slowing down expansion?" and just remove it — that's a much more efficient locust than anything nature produced.

So I don't think it's inevitable. I think there are plausible worlds where some single actor gets a big enough head start that it never faces competition, or where there's a genuine agreement with teeth. But those are the exceptions you'd have to argue for. The default, if you just let a competitive process run with variation and heritability, is that the thing optimised for spreading is what you end up with. And I guess I'd put it as: it's not that I'm confident the locusts win. It's that I don't see why anyone's confident they don't, and that's the thing that worries me about treating space as some kind of free lunch where there's room for everyone's values.

r001.rationale: The response discusses expanding agents and civilizations in space, but does not say that historically expansionist human societies tended to dominate more sedentary societies.

r002.rationale: It explains that selection in a competitive process favors agents that devote more resources to expansion, whose descendants then compound that advantage.

astra-6.text:
Well, I don’t think you have to assume that everyone wants to turn the universe into copies of themselves. You just need some group that does, and that’s willing to devote more of its resources to expansion than its neighbours are.

There’s a selection effect here. If you look at who gets to an unsettled solar system first, it’s going to disproportionately be the people who prioritised getting there quickly and sending out the next wave. They might be a tiny minority of the original civilisation, but they could end up controlling most of the territory.

And they don’t necessarily have to be aggressive. Even if they respect everyone else’s property, they can still take most of what nobody owns yet. The people who want to stay home and have wonderful lives can do that, but their preferences won’t determine what happens across most of the universe.

That’s not an argument that this outcome is inevitable. Maybe expansion can be coordinated or constrained. But I don’t think it’s crazy to worry that competition rewards expansion itself, rather than whatever we would actually want all those resources to be used for.

r001.rationale: The response says those who prioritize reaching unsettled systems quickly and sending out further waves can end up controlling most of the territory, while people who stay home do not determine what happens across most of the universe.

r002.rationale: It describes a selection effect: settlers who prioritize rapid expansion are disproportionately first to new systems and can dominate territory, framing competition as rewarding expansion.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I don’t think it’s inevitable, but there’s a fairly straightforward selection argument. Suppose you have lots of different civilizations, or descendants of a civilization, with different preferences. Some want to stay put and have a nice life. Others want to turn every available resource into more copies of themselves and keep expanding. The second group is going to account for more and more of the settled universe, even if almost nobody initially wanted that outcome.

And they don’t necessarily have to win a war against everyone else. They can just get to unoccupied resources first. If you spend a thousand years deciding what a flourishing civilization should look like, while somebody else sends out probes that build more probes, that delay could have a lasting cost.

The important caveat is that this depends on what coordination is possible and what the actual advantages of expansion are. Maybe civilizations can enforce agreements, or expansion has diminishing returns. But I don’t think we can simply assume that because most people would prefer a rich, diverse future, competition will deliver one. The things that spread most successfully needn’t be the things we most value.

r001.rationale: The response compares expanding civilizations with those that stay put, but does not state that human societies historically effective at expanding tended to dominate more sedentary societies.

r002.rationale: It explains that selection favors civilizations that expand and make more copies, so they come to account for more of the settled universe.
